en.question: An approved decision uses an overnight Claude digest for supplier exceptions because discovery estimated fewer than 1% required same-hour action. The record names the operations director as owner and a rise above 5% as a review trigger. A representative pilot measures 12%; same-hour cases lose value overnight. Costs still favor batching, and no production incident has occurred. What should the architect communicate?

options.text: The assumption and review trigger have failed; ask the owner to compare timely alternatives, including a separate urgent path, using the pilot evidence.
options.note: The documented trigger requires reopening the timeliness trade-off before an incident, while leaving the choice of alternative to the authorized decision process.

options.text: The decision remains valid because batching is still cheapest; document the urgent cases as users whose requests fall outside the original service.
options.note: The new evidence concerns the intended workload and violates the recorded assumption; excluding those users would conceal the failed requirement.

options.text: The pilot validates a lower-cost architecture; keep the decision and defer the timeliness discussion until a customer submits a confirmed incident.
options.note: The explicit evidence-based trigger does not depend on an incident, and known loss of timeliness is already relevant to the business outcome.

options.text: The architect should replace batching with a real-time agent immediately and update the owner after deployment because the trigger has been crossed.
options.note: A review trigger authorizes reconsideration, not an unreviewed replacement whose cost, risk, and operational needs have not been compared.

references.title: Anthropic Partner Academy: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM
